title: The language of contracts
goal: Find your way around an Indonesian legal text — an MoU, a regulation, a contract — and unpack its fixed formulas. Then do the more useful thing: ask a lawyer what a clause actually means, and say it back in plain Indonesian.
bekal: navigate a legal document by *pasal*, *ayat* and *huruf*, and cite a clause the Indonesian way: *Pasal 7 ayat (3)*
decode the formulas *sebagaimana dimaksud*, *terhitung sejak*, *dalam hal*, *yang bersangkutan*, *tanpa mengurangi*
turn legalese into everyday Indonesian and check your understanding: *Dengan kata lain…*, *Maksudnya…?*

notes: **Pasal, ayat, huruf.** An Indonesian legal text is built like a set of boxes: *bab* (chapter) contains *pasal* (article), a *pasal* contains numbered *ayat* (paragraphs, written *(1)*, *(2)*), and an *ayat* may contain lettered *huruf* (points *a.*, *b.*). You cite them from big to small with no commas: *Pasal 7 ayat (3) huruf b*. Attachments are *lampiran*.

**Nota kesepahaman and PKS.** The MoU is the umbrella: it states intent and scope, and usually carries no budget. The binding detail — money, deliverables, deadlines — lives in the *perjanjian kerja sama* (PKS) that follows. In speech everyone says *MoU* (em-o-yu); on paper the Indonesian name is used.

**Sebagaimana dimaksud** is the most frequent phrase in Indonesian law: “as referred to”. The drafting convention is precise: *pada* for a paragraph inside the same article (*sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1)*), *dalam* for another article (*sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 3*). Get that little preposition right and your drafts will look professionally made.

**Terhitung sejak** means “counting from”: the period starts on that day. The civil service writes it as *terhitung mulai tanggal*, abbreviated **TMT**, which you will find on every appointment letter. Its partner at the other end is *sampai dengan* (s.d.), “up to and including”.

**60 (enam puluh).** Numbers and sums of money in contracts are written twice, in digits and then in words in brackets: *Rp10.000.000,00 (sepuluh juta rupiah)*. Fajar's reason is the real one: a *6* can become an *8* with one stroke of a pen, *enam* cannot become *delapan*.

💬 **Fajar's Betawi.** *Udeh* = *sudah*, *kagak* = *tidak*, *tebel* = *tebal*, *dipalsuin* = *dipalsukan* (the Jakarta *-in* replacing *-kan*), *mending* = *lebih baik*. He reads the clauses aloud in flawless baku and comments on them in Betawi — which is exactly how Jakarta offices sound.

grammars.title: The fixed formulas of a clause
body: Legal Indonesian is repetitive on purpose: the same phrase always means the same thing, so nobody can argue about it later. Learn these seven and most clauses stop being frightening.

head: Formula
What it does
Example
rows: a case that may or may not happen

after: *Dalam hal* deserves attention because English speakers read it as “in the matter of”. In a clause it means “in the event that”, and it is the drafting guidelines' own choice for a situation that might never arise.

⚠️ *Yang bersangkutan* is not only legal. Every certificate from a village office ends *Surat keterangan ini dibuat untuk dipergunakan oleh yang bersangkutan* — “for the use of the person named”. In speech it can be mildly ironic: *Yang bersangkutan belum datang* = “His Lordship hasn't turned up yet”.

grammars.title: Wajib, harus, dapat, berhak: the modal verbs of law
body: In everyday Indonesian *harus* and *wajib* are near-synonyms and *dapat* just means “can”. In drafting each one has a job, and misreading them misreads the whole clause.

head: Word
Legal meaning
Example
rows: a requirement (not met, you don't get something)

after: ⚠️ *Dapat* in a contract is permission, not ability. *Pihak Pertama dapat menunda pembayaran* does not describe what the first party is physically capable of; it gives them the right to delay payment. That single word has cost people money.
*Tidak dapat diganggu gugat* — “cannot be challenged” — closes many official decisions. It sounds like a threat and is meant to.

dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon. Ratih Kusumawardani, S.H., the foundation's legal adviser, joins Sarah in the meeting room with the marked-up draft.

notes: **Bu Sarah, not Mbak Sarah.** In Yogyakarta Sarah was *Mbak* to everyone, and inside her own team Fajar and Yoga still call her that. To lawyers and ministries, as a programme director, she has become *Bu* (from *Ibu*), and so has everyone of her rank. It is not about age; it is about role, and being called *Mbak* in a formal meeting would now sound almost cheeky.

**Apabila and jika.** Both mean “if”. The official drafting guidelines reserve *jika* for conditions and *apabila* for “when”, but real contracts use them loosely, and *apabila* is more common in formal speech. In conversation you will just hear *kalau*.

**Musyawarah untuk mufakat** — deliberation until everyone agrees — is written into Pancasila and into almost every Indonesian contract. It is not decoration: courts and ministries really do expect parties to have talked first. Going straight to court is seen as aggressive.
**Bunyinya** is “its wording”, from *bunyi* (sound). *Pasal 3 berbunyi…* = “Article 3 reads…”. It is the natural way to ask for or introduce the exact text of a clause, a slogan or a text message.

**Dengan kata lain** (“in other words”) is the learner's best friend in any technical conversation. Rephrase what you heard, and the other person will confirm or correct you. Alternatives: *Jadi, intinya…* (so basically…) and *Kalau saya tidak salah tangkap…* (if I've understood correctly…).

**Tanpa mengurangi** is literally “without reducing” and corresponds to the English legal “without prejudice to”. Its cousin *dengan tetap memperhatikan* (“while still observing”) does the same job. Both tell you that one clause sits on top of another without cancelling it.

grammars.title: From legalese to plain Indonesian
body: What Sarah did with *Dengan kata lain* is the core skill of this unit: read the formal version, then say it the way a person would. The meaning must not change; only the register does.
after: Notice how legal Indonesian inflates verbs into phrases: *menempuh jalur mediasi* (“take the mediation path”) rather than *memediasi*, *memberitahukan secara tertulis* rather than *menyurati*. Unit 2's advice on *kalimat efektif* does not apply to contracts; lawyers prefer the long form because it is the one courts already know.

sections.title: The anatomy of an official document

blocks.text: Regulations, decrees (*surat keputusan*, SK) and contracts all follow the same skeleton. Once you know it you can find the part that matters — usually the *batang tubuh* — without reading every *menimbang*.

head: Part
Starts with
What it contains
rows: the reasons, each one a *bahwa* clause

blocks.title: Who is who in a contract
items: *Pihak Pertama* and *Pihak Kedua* — the First and Second Party, capitalised, defined once at the top and never named again.
*para pihak* — the parties together; *masing-masing pihak* — each party.
*pihak ketiga* — a third party, anyone outside the agreement.
*kuasa hukum* — legal representative; *saksi* — witness; *materai* (standard spelling *meterai*) — the duty stamp that makes a private document admissible.

blocks.text: The same vocabulary spills into letters, certificates and office life. These are the words you will meet at Imigrasi, at the bank and on every *surat keterangan*.

⚠️ In speech almost everyone says *legalisir* (“ijazahnya sudah dilegalisir?”); the standard word is *legalisasi*, verb *melegalisasi*. Likewise *materai* is what people write on the shop sign, *meterai* is what KBBI accepts. Use the spoken forms at the counter and the standard ones in writing.
